references.text: Herod Antipas is mentioned as tetrarch of Galilee ([ref:Luk 3:1|Luke 3:1]). Pilate recognized that Jesus belonged to Herod's jurisdiction as a Galilean and therefore sent him to Herod.
In [ref:Luk 23:6|Luke 23:6], Pilate asks whether Jesus is from Galilee, which forms the basis for the decision to send him on to Herod, who had authority over Galilee.

In [ref:Luk 23:8-12|Luke 23:8-12], the subsequent meeting between Jesus and Herod in Jerusalem is described, where Herod questions Jesus and finally sends him back to Pilate. The verses also state that Pilate and Herod became friends that day.
Herod had already heard about Jesus earlier and was amazed by him ([ref:Luk 9:7-9|Luke 9:7-9]). His desire to see Jesus forms the background for the meeting now taking place in Jerusalem.

In [ref:Luk 13:31-32|Luke 13:31-32], some Pharisees warn Jesus that Herod intends to kill him. Jesus calls Herod "that fox", which shows the hostile relationship between them and provides context for this meeting.

In [ref:Apg 4:27|Acts 4:27], the early church refers to how "Herod and Pontius Pilate" together with the Gentiles and the people of Israel gathered against Jesus. This confirms the cooperation between Pilate and Herod in the trial of Jesus.
The Mosaic law in [ref:5 Mos 21:22|Deuteronomy 21:22] deals with execution and the legal process. Pilate's transfer of the case to Herod reflects an acknowledgment of jurisdictional principles.
In [ref:Apg 25:6-12|Acts 25:6-12], Paul appeals to the emperor, another example of jurisdictional issues in Roman legal practice, parallel to Pilate's transfer of Jesus' case to Herod.
